To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) the pharmacodynamic model equation fitted to the killing curves of MPM or CLC against two strains of S. aureus in vitro predicted well the killing at different antibiotic concentrations, (ii) the in vivo killing of S. aureum was well predicted by the in vitro killing, and (iii) the in vivo growth of S. aureuim was the main determinant of the proportionality factor.

the pharmacodynamic model of MPM and CLC against S. aureus is valid both in vitro and in an experimental infection and that killing rate in an experimental infection is proportional to the killing rate in vitro.

the pharmacodynamic model equation fitted well to the numbers of bacteria, the EC50s of the two antibiotics were similar, the in vivo killing was well predicted from the in vitro killing, and there was no difference in killing between the antibiotics.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a model to describe the in vitro and in vivo efficacies of antibiotics.
a pharmacodynamic model for the effects of antibiotics on bacterial numbers.
pharmacokinetic and pharmacodynamics of antibiotics in vitro and in vivo.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a pharmacodynamic model equation can be fitted to the in vitro data for MPM and CLC and that this equation can be used to predict in vitro numbers of CFU with satisfactory precision.

the pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic models for the efficacies of MPM and CLC against S. aureus in vitro and in vivo were adequate and that there were no differences between the antibiotics or strains.
the pharmacodynamics model is applicable for both MPM and CLC, but that the proportionality factor is strain and animal specific and cannot be determined from in vitro experiments alone.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the model equation, which is based on a concentration-dependent killing rate, is useful for predicting numbers of CFU in vitro, and that in vivo, the killing rate is proportional to that observed in vitro, with a proportionality factor that varies with growth rate.
the killing rates of both antibiotics in vitro were well described by the pharmacodynamic model, and the model could be used to predict the effects in vivo.
the killing rate of MPM is 2.3 to 4.2 times higher than that of CLC against S. aureus.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the in vitro pharmacodynamics of MPM and CLC against S. aureus can be used to predict the efficacies of these antibiotics in an animal model.
the in vitro model is a useful tool for predicting the in vivo efficacy of an antibiotic against a specific strain.
the model can be used to predict the efficacies of antibiotics in vivo from in vitro data.
